title: How to Recognize When You Have Stopped Growing
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Notes piece argues that good leaders refuse to stay in a successful situation so long that success becomes stagnation. Stagnation rarely announces itself, because it arrives dressed as mastery, and the very signals leaders are trained to trust, smooth execution, fewer surprises and less prep time, are often the first evidence that growth has stopped. The author offers diagnostic signs: rarely being surprised by people or results, meetings that merely confirm what you already believe, the absence of pushback, long stretches without feeling clumsy or out of depth, and stories whose lessons have hardened into rules. The less flattering reading of fading pushback is that the leader has become too expensive to disagree with. The remedy runs against instinct: give away what you are best at and experiment with what you are bad at, placing yourself in rooms where you are the least experienced person.
points: Smooth execution, fewer surprises and less prep time can be early signs that learning has stopped rather than evidence of mastery.
A leader who is rarely surprised by a customer, colleague or result probably is not looking closely, since predictability can be intellectual hibernation.
When pushback fades it may mean not trust but that the leader has become too expensive to disagree with.
If a leader's best stories are years old and their lessons have hardened into defended rules, the past has begun to manage the present.
The remedy is to hand signature strengths to others and deliberately work in areas of weakness among people with more experience.
quotes: The trouble is that stagnation rarely announces itself. It arrives dressed as mastery, wearing the clothes of competence and walking with ease.
The very signals leaders are trained to trust, such as smooth execution, fewer surprises, and less prep time, are often the first evidence that learning and growth have quietly stopped.
When meetings mostly confirm what you already know and believe, and you can predict how most conversations will end before they begin, you are not seeing more clearly. You have stopped looking.
When pushback fades, many leaders conclude they have earned the trust of others. The less flattering explanation is that they have become too expensive to disagree with.
Leaders who haven’t felt clumsy, awkward, or out of their depth in months are likely spending their time inside their strengths.
When their best examples are years old and when the lessons of those stories have hardened into rules they defend rather than test, the past has begun to manage the present.
Leaders who want to keep growing must give away what they are best at and begin experimenting with what they are bad at.
